long_chip_timing.method: A long chip is one whose label goes through data-scroll-phase waiting, scrolling, end. 'Words stop' = the read where the phase first shows end. 'Starts to leave' = the first read where that chip's words element has been replaced (the label is a garbled decode text or a new chip). I did not find the slot's own opacity changing at all (reads of the slot's opacity stayed 1 the whole 200 s), so the 'opacity starts to fall' part could not be read; the replacement of the words is what I used.
long_chip_timing.values: 1122 to 1767 ms for 42 of the 44; the two others 3408 ms and 4566 ms. Values bunch at about 1140 ms (11 chips: 1122 to 1195) and about 1700 ms (31 chips: 1653 to 1767). One read takes about 572 ms, so each gap is only known to within one read: the 1140 ms group means a true gap between about 0.6 and 1.7 s, the 1700 ms group between about 1.1 and 2.3 s. The two groups are what a single steady gap of about 1.2 to 1.7 s would look like.
long_chip_timing.inside_1.2_to_1.9: 31 of 44 read inside 1.2 to 1.9 s; 11 read just under (1.12 to 1.20 s); 2 read over (3.4 s and 4.6 s).
long_chip_timing.the_two_long_ones: In both, the other chip slot changed at almost the same time and the row replaced that one first: 'How do I beat Dreadnought...' (slot 0) had its words stop at 59.5 s and the other slot swapped at 60.6 s, slot 0 itself left at 62.9 s. 'Any Steam Input issues for...' (slot 1): words stopped at 177.3 s, slot 0 swapped at 179.0 s, slot 1 left at 181.9 s. So a chip that wants to leave at the same moment as the other waits a turn.

verdict: UNCLEAR (timing): 31 of 44 gaps read 1.2 to 1.9 s, 11 read 1.12 to 1.20 s, 2 read 3.4 and 4.6 s.
